item.title: India's little-known minority - The Siddi and the Olympic dream | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Nimeksha Siddi is 18 years old and India's sprinting hope for the 2028 Olympics. Nimeksha belongs to the Siddi ethnic group, whose daily lives are marked by racism and exclusion.
The 18-year-old sprinter Nimeksha flies down the home straight like a bolt of lightning. She's a Siddi. Hardly anyone knows about her people, not even in India, where the Siddi have lived for 500 years. Her ancestors came to India from Africa as slaves or mercenaries. It's not known how many Siddi live in India. They all have the surname Siddi. They are Muslim, Christian or Hindu - and are often mistaken for tourists by many Indians. Most live in poverty, scraping by as day laborers, gathering plants, honey or rubber.
In 1983, India's Minister for Sport launched a program aimed at tapping into the community's athletic potential. Children from Siddi villages were recruited and coached in running. One of the most successful was Kamala Siddi. At the age of 15, she set a national record in the pentathlon, won bronze and gold at international level, and was rewarded with a job on the railways and a flat with running water.
Now her daughter Nimeksha is in the spotlight. She could become India's hope for the 2028 Olympic Games.

item.title: How dependent is Germany on skilled workers from abroad? | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
To what extent do German hospitals rely on foreign healthcare professionals? This film looks at expert opinions and the personal experiences of doctors from abroad, to highlight the structural challenges facing the German hospital system.
Germany is training more doctors than ever before - but the shortfall in hospitals still runs to thousands. The reason for this lies less in the absolute figures than in their distribution. Many specialists are drawn to urban centers, while rural areas face a shortage of skilled staff. Furthermore, many doctors are set to retire in the coming years, and an increasing number of them are working part-time. This is creating a noticeable shortage despite the high density of doctors, a problem exacerbated by a hospital system that's under financial pressure in many places. Although Germany has many hospitals by international standards, these include numerous small clinics in rural areas that are often barely profitable. To counteract this trend, a comprehensive hospital reform was launched at the end of 2024: fewer sites, greater specialization, and more outpatient treatment. While the Joint Federal Committee sees opportunities for greater efficiency in this move, the German Hospital Association warns that new gaps in care could arise in rural areas. The documentary follows Mohamed Cherbagi, an internist from Syria who most recently worked at a hospital in Freiberg, Saxony, and Ina Viaroukina from Belarus, a junior doctor at the Harzklinikum in Quedlinburg. Both are taking on roles in places where their German colleagues are becoming increasingly hard to find. Through their personal stories, along with insightful commentary from experts, the documentary shows just how dependent many hospitals are on doctors from abroad, and how this dependence is linked to the structural challenges facing the German hospital system.

This interview was recorded for the GOTO Book Club. #GOTOcon #GOTObookclub http://gotopia.tech/bookclub
Check out more here: https://gotopia.tech/episodes/454
Will Briggs - Professor of Computer Science at University of Lynchburg & Author of "C++26 for Lazy Programmers" Todd L. Montgomery - Software Professional & Advisor at DRW & Co-Author & Co-Maintainer of Aeron, Agrona & Simple Binary Encoding (SBE)
RESOURCES Will https://www.linkedin.com/in/will-briggs-32635714a https://www.lynchburg.edu/will-briggs
Todd https://twitter.com/toddlmontgomery https://www.linkedin.com/in/todd-montgomery-413a3216 https://github.com/tmontgomery
DESCRIPTION Will Briggs — a University of Lynchburg computer science professor with three decades of experience teaching C++ — joins Todd L. Montgomery to talk through C++26 for Lazy Programmers, and the conversation opens on the question every language-learning book has to answer right now: does learning a language still matter when AI writes so much of the code? Briggs' answer is refreshingly unhyped — he tests a new AI tool about once a year on a real, medium-difficulty problem, and as of this year's attempt, it still couldn't solve one, though it's genuinely useful for speeding up work he already understands. Both he and Montgomery land on the same practical conclusion: reading code fluently matters more now, not less, because code is increasingly how AI communicates back to you, and you can't debug or direct what you can't read. The rest of the conversation is a genuine craft discussion about how to teach C++ well — sequencing concepts so a beginner never has to hold two new ideas at once, giving double duty to topics like operator overloading and custom string classes, and deliberately introducing pointers nineteen chapters before ever using the word "pointer", by building the underlying mental model through arrays first.
For engineers who've been away from C++ or are watching it from a distance, there are a few sharp, specific takeaways: Briggs points to AI-generated C++ as noticeably more reliable than AI-generated Java, plausibly because of training-corpus quality rather than anything about the language itself, and he's blunt about C++26's biggest usability problem being proliferation, not power — he cites a case of 25 different ways floating around online just to initialize a single number, and argues the language needs fewer new ways to do old things. He also makes a case, backed by the TIOBE index, that C — a language from 1972 — is still the second most popular language in the world, and that learning C++ specifically (precisely because it's hard and concept-dense) is some of the best preparation available for picking up nearly any other language quickly afterward.

Kaspar von Grünberg - Founder & CEO at Stealth & Author of "Thinking in Platforms" Luca Galante - Managing Director at Weave Intelligence & Co-Author of "Thinking in Platforms"
RESOURCES Kaspar https://www.linkedin.com/in/kvgruenberg https://github.com/Kasparvongruenberg https://kasparvongruenberg.com
Luca https://x.com/luca_cloud https://www.linkedin.com/in/luca-galante https://platformengineering.org/authors/luca-galante
Links @PlatformEngineering https://platformengineering.org https://youtu.be/hBxV3Cr0lXY https://youtu.be/aIWhbS6rv0k https://youtu.be/mRoWGqcBSzk
DESCRIPTION Kaspar von Grünberg and Luca Galante — co-authors of the new book Thinking in Platforms and co-founders of Humanitec and the PlatformEngineering.org community — trace their field back to an origin story most engineers will recognize: a company held hostage by a single backend engineer who could threaten to walk unless he got a 3x raise. That "key person dependency" problem, they argue, is exactly what industrialization solved a century earlier when Henry Ford moved manufacturing from artisan workshops to standardized assembly lines — and it's the same move platform engineering makes for software: treating the internal setup as a product instead of something that "just happens" to a team. The book is structured in three parts — historical foundations, a "path-to-outcome" conceptual framework built around golden paths, and a hands-on playbook for going from a minimum viable platform to full enterprise adoption — because, as they note, most platform efforts don't fail on the technical side; they fail on the social side, in getting buy-in from developers, executives, and security teams alike.
The conversation's sharpest point for engineers building with AI right now: agents make platforms non-optional, not less necessary. An AI agent dropped into an enterprise full of undocumented "tribal knowledge" fails for the same reason a new hire would — except at scale, and fast. Von Grünberg's analogy: it's like hiring a brilliant intern and sending them into an office where nobody speaks their language, then being surprised there's no output a week later. That means real infrastructure — context management, security, observability, governance — has to exist before agents can be productive, and the old rule of thumb that you needed 100+ developers to justify a platform team no longer applies when a single person can be running a thousand agents. The bigger claim: platform engineering is already spreading past IT into security, data, and eventually every knowledge-work function, becoming less a software discipline and more the operating model for AI-first organizations.

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb
And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate In November 2002, the oil tanker “Prestige” sank off the coast of Galicia in northwestern Spain after encountering a winter storm, causing one of the worst oil spills in the country’s history.
The tanker had a murky and complicated backstory — making it difficult to track culpability. At 26 years old, the rusting, single-hulled tanker was well past the age of retirement. But that didn’t deter the owners from loading the aging ship with crude oil number 4, one of the most toxic fuel oils known.
After the spill, Spain imposed a six-month ban on fishing in the region, leading to great economic hardship.
“Spain: The Lawless Sea” investigated what went wrong with the tanker and uncovered a largely unregulated maritime system that offered few safeguards against environmental disasters.
“This is an act of terror, a criminal act,” said Rafael Mouzo, a fisherman and then-mayor of the coastal town of Concurbion. “We need an international tribunal to judge ... all those responsible for the spill.”

item.title: Rivers under pressure - From drought and competing agendas | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Hotter temperatures, falling groundwater levels, and dry soil are putting pressure on Germany's water resources. Can plans to improve water retention and restore river landscapes solve the problem?
This documentary follows people who are fighting to secure the future of water resources in three German states. They range from scientists to farmers, to environmental groups, and politicians. We discover the consequences of decades of river straightening and hear why floodplains are so important for flood protection, drinking water supply, and climate adaptation. Using the examples of the Unstrut, Mulde, and Elbe rivers, the film illustrates the opportunities offered by renaturation projects as well as the divisions they can cause. Amid the tensions between nature conservation, agriculture, and political interests, one central question arises: How can Germany ensure more water is retained in the land in future?
